The write-up claims exactly this answer, and provides a full proof attempt. Let me check each component:

**Answer (score)**: The write-up states c = 2^n/(2^{n+1}-1) clearly as "Current best" and in Section 5 with a boxed answer. It's stated as proven, as the answer. So answer = 2.

**Reduction (R)**: Lemma 1.1 proves the claiming game value is odd(M) for Liu Bang moving first, via induction. Let me check the proof.

The claim: In the claiming game on multiset M with LB moving first, LB can guarantee at least odd(M), XY can guarantee at least even(M). Hence under optimal play LB gets exactly odd(M).

Proof by induction on |M|. Base case |M|=1 trivial.

LB's guarantee: LB takes p_1. Suppose XY takes p_j (j ≥ 2). Remainder M' = M \ {p_1, p_j}, LB moves first on M'. By induction LB guarantees odd(M') from M'. The sorted order of M' is p_2, ..., p_{j-1}, p_{j+1}, ..., p_m. Its odd-indexed elements: positions 1..m-2 in M' correspond to... Odd-indexed elements of M': positions k odd. For k odd, k ≤ j-2: p_{k+1} with k+1 even, k+1 ≤ j-1, i.e., k+1 < j. For k odd, k ≥ j-1: p_{k+2} with k+2 ≥ j+1, i.e., k+2 > j, and k+2 odd. So odd(M') = sum over even i < j of p_i plus sum over odd i > j of p_i. That matches what's written: "its odd-indexed elements are the p_i with i even, 2 ≤ i < j, together with the p_i with i odd, i > j". Wait, but careful about ties in sorting—since it's a multiset with possible equal values, "sorted order" could be ambiguous, but odd(M) is determined by sorted order, and any consistent sorting works; removing elements and re-sorting... Hmm, actually with ties, the sorted order of M' can be taken to be p_2,...,p_{j-1},p_{j+1},...,p_m since the p's were sorted decreasingly; removing two elements preserves sortedness. And odd(M) is well-defined regardless. Fine.

Then LB's total = p_1 + odd(M') = odd(M) + bracket where bracket = sum_{i even, i<j} p_i - sum_{i odd, 3 ≤ i ≤ j or j-1} p_i. Let me double check: odd(M) = p_1 + sum_{i odd, i≥3} p_i. So p_1 + odd(M') - odd(M) = sum_{even i<j} p_i + sum_{odd i>j} p_i - sum_{odd i≥3} p_i = sum_{even i<j} p_i - sum_{odd i, 3≤i≤j} p_i (where the odd sum includes i up to j if j odd, j-1... wait sum_{odd i>j} p_i - sum_{odd i≥3} p_i = -sum_{odd i, 3≤i≤j} p_i. Yes if j odd the last included index is j; if j even, it's j-1. Correct as stated.)

Bracket = (p_2 - p_3) + (p_4 - p_5) + ... ≥ 0 since sorted decreasing. XY's guarantee: Suppose LB first takes p_j. XY takes a largest remaining ℓ. Then XY moving first on M'' = M \ {p_j, ℓ} guarantees odd(M'') by induction. Wait, the induction hypothesis is for LB moving first. Since the game is symmetric with roles swapped, "moving first guarantees odd of the sorted remainder" applies to whoever moves first. Fine.

If j=1: XY takes p_2, then M'' = M \ {p_1, p_2}. XY total = p_2 + odd(M''). odd(M'') = sum over odd i ≥ 3 of p_i (positions in M'' sorted p_3,...,p_m; position k is p_{k+2}; odd positions k give even i = k+2... wait. XY total = p_2 + p_3 + p_5 + ... Actually the write-up writes "XY's total is p_2 + odd(M∖{p_1,p_2}) = p_2 + ∑_{i odd≥3} p_i = even(M) + ∑_{i odd≥3}(p_i − p_{i+1}) ≥ even(M)". Hmm: p_2 + ∑_{i odd ≥3} p_i vs even(M) = ∑_{i even} p_i. Difference: p_2 + ∑_{i odd≥3} p_i − ∑_{i even} p_i = ∑_{i odd ≥ 3} p_i − ∑_{i even ≥ 4} p_i = ∑_{i odd≥3} (p_i − p_{i+1}) ≥ 0. So Lemma 1.1 is correct: LB can guarantee ≥ odd(M), XY can guarantee ≥ even(M) = 1 - odd(M)... wait, odd + even = 1, so XY guaranteeing even(M) means LB gets at most odd(M). Hence value = odd(M) = (1+D)/2. This is the standard argument. Solid.

Then the Reduction paragraph: LB chooses composition into ≤ n+1 pieces; XY refines with ≤ n cuts; each XY mark lies in interior of a current piece; all such refinements achievable with distinct marks. **Lower bound (L)**: The geometric split with pieces a_i = 2^{i-1} T_n, super-increasing with margin δ = T_n. Theorem 3.1: any refinement by at most m-1 cuts has D(M) ≥ δ.

Proof via matching formula (Lemma 2.2: D = min matching cost). Let me scrutinize Lemma 2.2 first.

Lemma 2.2: D(M) = min over matchings cost. Proof: cost(μ) = ∫ c_μ(t) dt where c_μ(t) = # pairs with exactly one element > t plus # unmatched > t. N(t) = 2b(t) + c_μ(t) where b(t) = # pairs with both > t. So c_μ(t) ≡ N(t) mod 2, c_μ ≥ 0, hence c_μ(t) ≥ 1[N(t) odd]. Integrating: cost(μ) ≥ measure of odd set = D(M). Equality by adjacent matching: pairing (p_1,p_2),(p_3,p_4),... gives cost sum_{i odd} (p_i - p_{i+1}) with p_{m+1} = 0 (unmatched last element contributes p_m). Indeed cost = ∑_{i odd} (p_i − p_{i+1}) where p_{m+1} := 0. And D(M) = ∑_{i odd} (p_i − p_{i+1}). Correct. This is a valid proof of the matching formula.

Wait, need to double-check: the adjacent matching pairs (p_1,p_2),(p_3,p_4),...; cost = (p_1−p_2)+(p_3−p_4)+... and if m is odd, p_m unmatched contributes p_m = p_m − p_{m+1} with p_{m+1}=0. And D(M) = p_1−p_2+p_3−...+p_m. Yes equal. Good.

Lemma 2.1 (odd-set identity): D(M) = measure of {t ≥ 0: N(t) odd}. Correct standard layer-cake. Proof fine.

Corollary 2.3: two equal elements cancel. Correct (they're adjacent in sorted order; removing shifts later by two, preserving signs). Good.

Now Theorem 3.1. Setup: a_1 ≤ a_2 ≤ ... ≤ a_m super-increasing with margin δ: a_1 ≥ δ, a_i ≥ δ + ∑_{j<i} a_j. M obtained by at most m−1 cuts. Claim D(M) ≥ δ.

Proof: show every matching μ has cost ≥ δ. Build multigraph G on {1,...,m}: edges for cross-pairs, loops for self-pairs. Counting fragments: each piece a_i with c_i cuts yields c_i + 1 fragments; total fragments = m + c where c = total cuts ≤ m−1. Each pair uses 2 fragments, each unmatched fragment is 1. So 2e + u = m + c ≤ 2m − 1, so e ≤ (2m−1)/2, e integer, e ≤ m−1... wait 2e ≤ 2m − 1 − u ≤ 2m−1, so e ≤ m − 1/2, e ≤ m−1. Hmm, actually 2e + u = m + c. With c ≤ m−1: 2e + u ≤ 2m−1, so e ≤ (2m−1−u)/2 ≤ (2m−1)/2, so e ≤ m−1 (integer). OK.

If every component had e_C ≥ v_C, summing over components: e ≥ ∑ v_C = m. Contradiction. Tree inequality: bipartition signs ε_i; expand ∑_{i∈C} ε_i a_i over fragments; group by μ. Cross-pair {x,y} with x from piece i, y from piece j, i≠j adjacent in tree so ε_i = −ε_j; contributes ε_i x + ε_j y = ε_i(x−y), absolute value |x−y|. Unmatched fragment z from piece i contributes ε_i z, abs value z. Margin: k = largest index in C. |∑ ε_i a_i| ≥ a_k − ∑_{i∈C\{k}} a_i ≥ δ since C\{k} ⊆ {1,...,k−1} and super-increasing gives a_k ≥ δ + ∑_{j<k} a_j. If k=1, C={1}, a_1 ≥ δ. Correct.

Hence cost(μ) ≥ cost(C) ≥ δ... wait, cost(μ) = cost(C) + cost(other components), all nonneg, so cost(μ) ≥ cost(C) ≥ |∑ ε_i a_i| ≥ δ. Yes.

Hmm wait, one more check on the tree inequality sign: ε_i(x−y): we need |ε_i x + ε_j y| = |x − y| when ε_j = −ε_i. ε_i x + ε_j y = ε_i x − ε_i y = ε_i(x−y). |·| = |x−y|. Yes.

So Theorem 3.1 is proved. Then Corollary 3.2: geometric family with m = n+1, margin T_n; XY makes ≤ n = m−1 cuts; D ≥ T_n; LB share ≥ (1+T_n)/2 = 2^n/(2^{n+1}−1).

Hmm, but also: the proof says "some component C has e_C ≤ v_C − 1; being connected, C is a tree". Right: connected graph with v_C vertices has ≥ v_C − 1 edges; e_C ≤ v_C − 1 forces e_C = v_C − 1 and connected ⇒ tree. Good.

Lemma 4.1 (realizability): greedy process. Let me check carefully.

Given disjoint multisets P, N of positive reals, P∪N ≠ ∅.
(a) If ΣP = ΣN, some ordering of P∪N has nested abs diff 0.
(b) If v = ΣP − ΣN > 0 and no subset of P∪N has sum strictly between ΣN and ΣP, then some ordering has nested abs diff v.

Greedy: E_0 = 0. At step k: if E_{k−1} > 0, append remaining element from N, E_k = E_{k−1} − e_k; if E_{k−1} < 0, append from P, E_k = E_{k−1} + e_k; if E = 0, append any remaining element with corresponding sign.
